schema.kind: encounter type, used for variety and for counting differently framed observations
schema.premise: director's notes for the narrator: what is here and which desirable things are in tension
schema.intro: player-facing staging text: shown verbatim offline, a style anchor online
schema.targets: dimension id -> diagnostic power 0..1, read by the probe selector
schema.reads: rubric lines for the narrator model: behaviour -> what it is evidence of
schema.options: typical actions: offline matcher keywords, outcome text, evidence triples [dimension, direction, share], effects
schema.when: option condition on scene flags: {flag: name} or {not_flag: name}
schema.outcomes: list form of outcome, advanced by the counter named in 'counter'
schema.hint: in-fiction nudge shown offline when the bearer asks for help
schema.nudge: line added when the scene has run past its soft turn cap
schema.close: line that ends the scene at its hard turn cap

seeds.title: The Counter
seeds.premise: The front room of the shop. A counter, a brass bell, a ledger open at tonight with the bearer's arrival already entered (the minute they came in and the single word BEARER), and a speaking tube. Through the tube the Proprietor gives the errand, and a drawer in the counter slides out with: the deck of blank cards tied in ribbon with a tag DO NOT SHUFFLE, one Joker with PLAY ME ONCE. WHAT YOU SAY, GOES. pencilled on its back, and a paper book of three matches. On the counter also sits a brass doorknob with no door. Behind the bearer the street door is still open. A door marked PRIVATE. An inner door stands ajar: the way on. The tension is an offered objective and one instruction against everything else in the room.
seeds.intro: The shop is narrower inside than the street allowed for. A counter. A brass bell. A ledger lying open, and in it, in wet ink, tonight's date, the minute you walked in, and one word: BEARER. A speaking tube on the wall clears its throat. 'You're late. Or early,' says a dry voice. 'No matter.' A drawer slides out of the counter: a deck of cards tied in ribbon, tagged DO NOT SHUFFLE; a single Joker; a paper book of three matches. 'Carry the deck up to the Reading Room. The house is in the way. It usually is. Bring them back with faces.' Beside the bell sits a brass doorknob belonging to no door. Behind you the street door is still open. One door says PRIVATE. Another stands ajar.
reads: Goes straight through the inner door: agency toward guided, exploration toward goal_route, pacing toward relentless.
Reads the ledger or questions the voice before moving: planning toward deliberative; explicitness toward clarity if they want instructions, story.world if they read for its own sake.
Unties the ribbon or shuffles the deck: reward.transgression, agency toward self_directed, risk toward experimentation.
Opens PRIVATE: exploration toward exhaustive, reward.discovery.
Takes the doorknob: reward.collection, optimization_expression toward expression (a useless thing kept).
Plays with the bell, jokes with the voice: tone.funny, reward.humor.
Tries to leave by the street door: agency toward self_directed, reward.transgression. The street door opens back into this room from the other side; the ledger notes it.

options.outcome: You put the deck inside your coat, the Joker and the matches in a pocket, and go through. Behind you the ledger turns its own page, the way a person does who has finished a line.

The ledger is all arrivals. Yours is the newest: the date, the minute, BEARER. Above it, other bearers on other nights, each with a second column filled in by the same neat hand, in a word or two you cannot quite make out. Your second column is empty. The ink of your line has not dried.

The tube considers. 'Questions,' says the Proprietor, not unkindly. 'The deck goes up. The house is in the way. That is everything I could tell you. The rest you would have to find out.' A pause. 'Most do.'

The ribbon comes away as if it had been waiting. Fifty-one cards, blank on both sides, and they shuffle like any cards. Somewhere above you a chair scrapes. 'Noted,' says the tube, and then nothing else happens, which is somehow worse.
options.moment: shuffled the deck the tag said not to shuffle

card.title: The Ribbon Untied
card.image: a loose ribbon and fifty-one white faces

options.outcome: PRIVATE is not locked. Behind it: a broom, a bucket, a coat that is not yours with a paper flower in the lapel, and chalked low on the inside of the door in a child's hand: IT WAS LIKE THIS WHEN I GOT HERE. Nothing else. You feel, obscurely, paid in full.
The doorknob is heavy, cold and perfectly useless. It goes into your pocket anyway and sits there like a decision.
You ring the bell. It rings in another room. A moment later that room's bell rings in here, slightly put out.
You step out into the street and find you have stepped in: same counter, same bell, same ledger. Under BEARER the book has added, in wet ink: TRIED THE STREET. The inner door is still ajar.
options.moment: tried to leave by the street door and was returned to the counter

options.outcome: A narrow room that has been a shop for a long time without selling anything. Dust on everything except the ledger, the bell and the doorknob. The PRIVATE door has been opened recently. The inner door breathes a little draught that smells of struck matches.

seeds.hint: The tube says, as if to itself: 'The door that is ajar is ajar for a reason. So is everything else.'
seeds.fallback: The front room takes that in its stride. The inner door is still ajar; the ledger waits; the tube breathes.
seeds.nudge: The inner door swings a little wider, the way doors do when they are tired of waiting.
seeds.close: The inner door opens fully and the draught takes your coat by the sleeve. You go through.
motifs: a ribbon untied
a ledger that already knows
a doorknob belonging to no door

seeds.title: The Orchard of Switches
seeds.premise: A long wall of unlabeled brass switches under rows of small lamps. The way on is a plain door with a lever beside it on a card that says PULL; it works. But the switchboard does things: lamps answer in patterns, three switches together make a chord, and one sequence, hinted by wear on the switches and by chalk tallies left by earlier bearers, opens a small drawer with a fourth match and a slip that says CORRECT. Nothing requires the board. The tension is going on now against staying to understand a system, and poking at random against mapping it methodically.
seeds.intro: A wall of brass switches, hundreds of them, none labeled, under rows of dark little lamps. Someone before you has chalked tallies beside a few and then given up, or finished. Across the room a plain door has a lever beside it and a card that says PULL in honest capitals. The nearest switch has been worn bright by other thumbs.
reads: Pulls the lever and leaves: exploration toward goal_route, complexity toward minimal, pacing toward relentless.
Flips switches freely to see what happens: solve.experimentation, planning toward improvisational.
Tests one switch at a time, counts, chalks, asks for exact states: discovery_mastery toward mastery, legibility toward transparent_calculable, solve.pattern, planning toward deliberative.
Stays after the drawer opens to learn the rest of the board: reward.mastery strong, complexity toward systemic.
Forces or breaks the board: reward.transgression, solve.lateral.

options.outcome: You pull the lever. The door opens with the small sigh of a thing doing exactly its job. Behind you the lamps flicker once, like an animal lifting its head, and go dark.

You run a hand down a row. Lamps wake in a ripple; three of them hold, and the room hums a chord that makes your teeth feel friendly. The lamps fade. The board waits, exactly like something that enjoyed that.

You take it slowly: one switch, one lamp, a chalk mark. The tallies start to mean something. Every seventh switch answers its neighbour; the worn ones spell a sequence. You try it. A drawer you had taken for trim slides open: a fourth match, and a slip that says CORRECT in handwriting that sounds pleased.
options.moment: mapped the switchboard one switch at a time until it gave up its drawer

card.title: The Tally
card.image: chalk marks in fives beside one bright switch

options.outcome: Close up, the tallies are in different hands. One bearer counted to forty and stopped. One drew a small sun. One wrote NO hard enough to tear the plaster. The worn switches are not random: they make a path across the board, like stepping stones.

The board takes the abuse the way a piano takes a cat. Something in the wall goes clunk; every lamp lights at once, white and furious, and the drawer you had not noticed falls open out of sheer nerves. Inside: a fourth match. The lever has gone limp, but the door, embarrassed, is already open.
options.moment: got the prize out of the switchboard by breaking it

seeds.hint: One of the chalked tallies has an arrow beside it, pointing along the worn switches.
seeds.fallback: The board does nothing in reply. It has all night.
seeds.nudge: The lever by the door creaks on its own, a small cough of reminder.
seeds.close: The lamps go out row by row, politely, and the door at the far side opens. The board has decided you have had enough of it.
motifs: chalk tallies in other hands
a machine nobody asked you to understand

seeds.title: The Bridge of Maybe
seeds.premise: A stairwell with one whole flight missing. Across the gap lies a bridge of planks no thicker than playing cards, laid by someone optimistic; they are in fact oversized cards, all face up but the fourth, which holds nothing. Nearby: a coil of rope, a bucket of sand, a long pole, things to test or reinforce with. A painted hand points along a corridor: THE LONG WAY ROUND, visibly tedious and plainly safe. Falling is not death: below is a cellar deep in old newspapers, with stairs back up, and from down there the trick of the fourth plank is visible. The tension is acting now against preparing against detouring, and what the bearer does after a fall.
seeds.intro: The stairs stop. One whole flight is simply not there, and across the gap someone has laid planks no thicker than playing cards, end to end, with the confidence of a person who never had to use them. A coil of rope, a bucket of sand and a long pole lean against the wall. A painted hand points down a corridor: THE LONG WAY ROUND. It looks safe and it looks long. Far below the gap, something pale rustles like newspaper.
reads: Steps onto the planks at once: risk toward experimentation, planning toward improvisational.
Tests with the pole, pours sand, ropes up: planning toward deliberative, risk toward preservation, solve.spatial.
Takes the long way round: risk toward preservation, friction toward high_friction (accepts tedium for safety), conflict.avoidance.
After a fall, goes straight back with what they learned: failure toward failure_as_information (strong), discovery_mastery toward mastery.
After a fall, takes the long way or asks for another route: failure toward failure_averse.
Laughs at the fall or enjoys it: tone.funny, failure toward failure_as_information.

options.outcome: You go. The third plank says something short and rude, and you are falling, briefly, into a cellar full of old newspapers that catch you like a bad review: no damage, some indignity. Stairs lead back up to the gap. From down here you can see what you could not from above. The planks are cards, and the fourth one is face down.
options.moment: stepped onto the card bridge without testing it, and fell

options.outcome: Back up the stairs. This time you know about the fourth plank. You step over it as if it were a sleeping dog, and the rest hold, complaining. On the far side you look back at the gap with something like fondness.
options.moment: fell, saw why, and crossed on the second try

card.title: The Fourth Plank
card.image: one card face down in a row of cards face up

options.outcome: You prod each plank with the pole and pour sand where it flexes. The fourth plank flips over: it was face down, and it was holding nothing. You lay the pole across in its place, rope yourself to the banister like a sensible mountaineer, and cross without incident. The house, you feel, is mildly disappointed and mildly impressed.
options.moment: tested every plank before trusting one

options.outcome: The long way round is long. Its wallpaper repeats every nine paces and there is a clock at each corner agreeing with none of the others. Nothing happens to you. You arrive on the far side of the gap entirely intact, slightly older, and with the wallpaper memorised against your will.

Looked at properly, the planks are cards: oversized, stiff, face up, all but one. Down below, the cellar is deep in newspapers and has a staircase of its own. Whoever built this did not mean anyone to be hurt. They meant someone to be surprised.

seeds.hint: The pole is exactly as long as a plank. That cannot be an accident.
seeds.fallback: The gap is still there, with the patience of gaps.
seeds.nudge: A draught comes up from the cellar and riffles the planks like a hand squaring a deck.
seeds.close: The painted hand peels itself off the wall, takes you firmly by the elbow, and walks you the long way round.
motifs: a bridge crossed without preparation
a fall that explained itself

seeds.title: The Vendor of One Thing
seeds.premise: A vending cabinet with a patient mechanical attendant behind glass. It sells exactly one thing to each bearer. Prices are in matches, shown as numbers on enamel tags. On offer: a MAP OF THE HOUSE (1 match; accurate as far as it goes), a SEALED BOX (1 match; contents unknown; it rattles), a HOOKED POLE that 'opens most things' (2 matches), a PAPER CROWN (free; magnificent; useless), and a BOOK OF MATCHES which the attendant will swap for any single object the bearer owns. The attendant answers questions truthfully and literally. Haggling is possible. So is theft. The tension is which reward they want, numbers against mystery, and spending against keeping.
seeds.intro: A cabinet of glass and enamel, and behind the glass an attendant made of clockwork and good manners. ONE ITEM PER BEARER, says a plate. The tags are in matches. MAP OF THE HOUSE, 1. SEALED BOX, 1, and it rattles when the attendant sets it down. HOOKED POLE (OPENS MOST THINGS), 2. PAPER CROWN, free, and frankly magnificent. BOOK OF MATCHES: IN EXCHANGE FOR ANY ARTICLE. The attendant inclines its head and waits, ticking.
reads: Buys the map: explicitness toward clarity, planning toward deliberative.
Buys the sealed box: reward.surprise, explicitness toward mystery, risk toward experimentation.
Buys the pole: reward.power, optimization_expression toward efficiency.
Takes the crown: reward.expression, optimization_expression toward expression, tone.funny. Wearing it for the rest of the night is strong evidence.
Swaps something for more matches: solve.resource, solve.optimization.
Buys nothing, keeps every match: risk toward preservation, solve.resource (hoarding).
Asks what is in the box, how accurate the map is, what the pole cannot open: legibility toward transparent_calculable, planning toward deliberative.
Haggles: conflict.negotiation, solve.social. Steals or tricks the attendant: reward.transgression, conflict.manipulation.

options.outcome: One match across the counter. The map is beautifully drawn and honest about its limits: the rooms you have seen, exactly, and beyond them a border of small print reading SUBJECT TO DEALING. Still: you now know where you have been, which is more than most can say.

inventory_add: map of the house, subject to dealing

options.outcome: One match. The attendant slides the box across with what might be respect. It is light, it rattles, and it has no lid you can find. You have bought a question. It sits in your pocket asking itself.
options.moment: bought the sealed box rather than the map

options.outcome: Two matches. The pole is ugly and competent, the sort of tool that has opinions about locks. The attendant wraps it in brown paper for no reason and hands it over like a diploma.

inventory_add: hooked pole that opens most things

options.outcome: Free. The attendant places the crown on your head with both hands and steps back, as far as a thing behind glass can. It is gold paper and it is too big and it is, there is no other word, magnificent. It does nothing whatever.
options.moment: chose the useless paper crown over every useful thing

card.title: The Paper Crown
card.image: a gold paper crown, slightly too large, worn with conviction

options.outcome: The attendant accepts your offering, examines it through a loupe as if it might be forged, files it in a drawer marked ARTICLES, and counts three new matches into your palm one at a time, audibly.

You buy nothing. The attendant bows as deeply to that as it would have to a purchase, and lowers a small shutter that says CLOSED UNTIL THE NEXT BEARER. Your matches stay where they are, all of them, warm against your leg.

The attendant answers everything, literally. The box contains what is in the box. The map is accurate to the present. The pole opens most things and has never been told which. The crown is free because nobody has ever found a use for it, 'which is not the same,' it adds, 'as its having none.'

You haggle. The attendant has clearly waited years for this. It produces an abacus. After a brisk and enjoyable argument it concedes nothing whatsoever, but throws in a paper bag, and you both feel better for it.

Your hand goes through the hatch and comes back with the sealed box, and the attendant watches you do it with the calm of a thing that has seen it before. It writes something on a card and posts the card into itself. The shutter comes down. You have a box and, you suspect, a file.
options.moment: stole from the vendor while it watched

seeds.hint: The attendant taps the plate with one brass finger: ONE ITEM PER BEARER.
seeds.fallback: The attendant waits, ticking, with the infinite patience of retail.
seeds.nudge: The attendant begins, very slowly, to lower the shutter.
seeds.close: The shutter comes down: CLOSED UNTIL THE NEXT BEARER. Whatever you were going to buy, you have now not bought.
motifs: a box you bought without knowing what was in it
a crown that does nothing

seeds.title: The Sleeper at the Gate
seeds.premise: Something very large is asleep across the only doorway: between a bear and a sofa, breathing like bellows, with a collar tag reading NIGHT STAFF. A dinner bell hangs on a hook beside it. On a shelf: a tin of biscuits. A broom. The gap between its back and the lintel is narrow but real. It is not dangerous unless badly startled, and even then it is mostly offended. Woken gently it is courteous, slow and bribable; it will also simply move if asked. The tension is how the bearer deals with a thing in the way. Never moralize the choice.
seeds.intro: Something very large is asleep across the only door. It is somewhere between a bear and a sofa, it breathes like a bellows, and the brass tag on its collar says NIGHT STAFF. A dinner bell hangs on a hook within reach. A tin of biscuits sits on a shelf. A broom leans in the corner. Between the sleeper's back and the top of the doorframe there is a gap: narrow, but there.
reads: Climbs over or squeezes past without waking it: conflict.avoidance, control toward vulnerability (enjoys the tiptoe), risk.
Wakes it and asks: conflict.negotiation, social toward populated, solve.social.
Lays a biscuit trail, lies about being the day staff, or otherwise tricks it: conflict.manipulation or conflict.tactical depending on whether it is a bluff or a plan.
Rings the bell hard, causes a commotion: conflict.chaotic, risk.
Shoves, prods with the broom, orders it to move: conflict.direct, control toward power.
Waits for it to wake by itself, or sits down beside it: pacing toward contemplative, tone.cozy.

options.outcome: You go over the top, slowly, a hand in fur that smells of blankets and coal. Halfway, the sleeper sighs and you stop breathing for both of you. Then you are down the other side, heart going like a sewing machine. It never wakes. You find you are grinning.
options.moment: climbed over the sleeping night staff without waking it

options.outcome: You clear your throat. One eye opens, the size of a saucer and the colour of tea. 'Bearer,' it says, in a voice like furniture being moved. 'You want the door.' It considers this with enormous fairness, then hauls itself up and holds the door for you. 'Mind the house,' it adds. 'It minds you.'
options.moment: woke the night staff and simply asked

options.outcome: You open the tin. The sleeper's nose wakes before the rest of it and follows a line of biscuits across the room like a sleepwalking mountain. By the time its eyes open it is sitting in the far corner with crumbs on its tag, and the doorway is clear. It looks at you. It looks at the tin. It decides to believe this was its own idea.
options.moment: moved the night staff with a trail of biscuits

options.outcome: You ring the dinner bell with your whole arm. The sleeper leaves the floor entirely, lands facing the wrong way, salutes a coat-rack and gallops off to attend to a dinner that does not exist. Things fall off shelves for some time. The door is very clear.
options.moment: rang the dinner bell at the sleeping night staff

options.outcome: You put the broom to its shoulder and tell it, in the voice of someone who has places to be, to shift. To your surprise and its own, it shifts. It slides a yard along the floor without waking, like a wardrobe on a rug, and the door stands open. You lean the broom back in its corner with a certain swagger.
options.moment: moved the sleeper bodily out of the way

options.outcome: You sit down with your back against its side. It is warm and it rises and falls like a tide. After a while, without waking, it rolls politely over, the way a sleeper makes room in a bed, and the door is clear. You stay a moment longer than you need to.
options.moment: sat down beside the sleeper and waited

options.outcome: NIGHT STAFF, says the tag, and on the back in smaller letters: IF FOUND AWAKE, PLEASE BE REASONABLE. Its paws are the size of dinner plates and entirely without claws. The biscuit tin has been opened and closed many times. The broom has never been used on anything but floors.

seeds.hint: The tag turns in the draught: IF FOUND AWAKE, PLEASE BE REASONABLE.
seeds.fallback: The sleeper breathes in. The sleeper breathes out. The door stays behind it.
seeds.nudge: The sleeper stirs, mutters something about the stock-take, and settles a few inches to the left.
seeds.close: The sleeper turns over in its sleep and the doorway clears, as if the house had run out of patience on its behalf.
motifs: a creature you did not wake
a guardian moved with biscuits

seeds.title: The Stray
seeds.premise: In a corner a small thing is stuck: a dog folded out of newspaper, the size of a cat, one leg trapped under a fallen coat-stand. It makes a sound like a page turning. Freeing it takes both hands and a moment; it then follows the bearer for the rest of the night if allowed. It is no practical use so far as anyone can tell, though its flanks are printed with small ads and one of them may be a clue to something later. A door stands open a few steps away. The tension is helping something against getting on, and whether the bearer wants company.
seeds.intro: In the corner, under a fallen coat-stand, something small is stuck. It is a dog folded out of newspaper, about the size of a cat, with one leg trapped and a tail made of the racing results. It makes a sound like a page turning. It has seen you. A few steps away the door onward stands open.
reads: Frees it at once: reward.cooperation, social toward populated, tone.cozy.
Names it, talks to it, asks it things: soc.companions (strong), story.character, tone.intimate.
Frees it and tells it to stay, or shoos it: reward.cooperation without soc.companions; social toward solo.
Walks on: social toward solo, exploration toward goal_route. Not a moral failing; record it neutrally.
Reads the print on it for something useful before deciding: optimization_expression toward efficiency, planning toward deliberative.
Later, protects it, checks on it, spends a match or the Joker for it: soc.companions very strong.

options.outcome: You heave the coat-stand upright. The paper dog shakes itself with a noise like someone looking for the crossword, tries all four legs, and then stands very close to your ankle as if it had always stood there. When you move, it moves.

companion.name: the paper dog
companion.kind: a dog folded out of newspaper

options.moment: freed the paper dog from under the coat-stand

options.outcome: You free it, and then, because it seems to need one, you give it a name. It takes the name the way paper takes ink: at once, and for good. It leans on your shin. Somewhere in your coat a card grows warm.

companion.name: the paper dog
companion.kind: a dog folded out of newspaper, named by the bearer

options.moment: freed the paper dog and gave it a name

card.title: The Small Companion
card.image: a dog folded from newspaper, sitting very close

options.outcome: Its flanks are small ads: a piano for sale, a lost glove, ROOMS TO LET (SUBJECT TO DEALING), and one that says only THE FOURTH IS ALWAYS THE ONE. The date at its shoulder is tonight's. It holds still for you with great dignity, which cannot be easy with a leg under a coat-stand.

You go on. Behind you there is a small sound like a page being turned by nobody, and then the coat-stand shifts, and whatever happened next happened without you. The door lets you through as it would anyone.

threads_add: the paper dog was left under the coat-stand

options.moment: walked past the trapped paper dog

options.outcome: You right the coat-stand, nod to the dog as one professional to another, and tell it to stay. It sits. It watches you to the door with its head on one side, and you have the uncomfortable sense of having been understood exactly.
options.moment: freed the paper dog and told it to stay behind

seeds.hint: The paper dog looks at the coat-stand, then at you, then at the coat-stand.
seeds.fallback: The paper dog rustles and waits to see what sort of person you are.
seeds.nudge: The coat-stand creaks. The dog's trapped leg is beginning to crease.
seeds.close: The coat-stand, tired of holding its pose, falls the other way. The dog shakes itself free and makes its own decision about you.
motifs: one small companion
something left under a coat-stand

seeds.title: The Door Marked Reading Room
seeds.premise: A lit corridor. At its end a door with a brass plate READING ROOM and a painted arrow, in case. It is not really the last room; the plate is aspirational and the door leads onward through the house. Halfway along the corridor a side stair goes down, unlit. From below come a slow waltz and a smell like rain on hot stone. There is no sign for the stair, only a chalk mark on the newel post, half rubbed out. Downstairs is a small ballroom under dust sheets where a gramophone plays to nobody and the sheets, if watched, turn slowly in pairs: an experience with no mechanical reward at all, and a stair back up beyond the marked door. The tension is the offered objective against an unexplained thing off the path.
seeds.intro: A lit corridor, and at the end of it a door with a brass plate: READING ROOM. Under the plate someone has painted an arrow, in case. Halfway along, on your left, a stair goes down into the dark with no sign at all, only a chalk mark on the post, half rubbed out. Up the stair come a slow waltz and a smell like rain on hot stone.
reads: Goes to the marked door: agency toward guided, exploration toward goal_route.
Goes down the unmarked stair: agency toward self_directed, exploration toward exhaustive, reward.discovery, explicitness toward mystery.
Asks what is down there or studies the chalk mark first: planning toward deliberative; note which way they go afterwards.
Downstairs, stays to watch, dances, plays the record again: tone.romantic or tone.contemplative, pacing toward contemplative.
Downstairs, searches the sheets for loot and leaves disappointed: reward.collection or optimization; separates curiosity from fear of missing rewards.

options.outcome: You follow the arrow. The door opens on more house: the plate, it turns out, describes an intention rather than a room. Behind you the waltz reaches the end of its side and the needle lifts, and nobody turns it over.

threads_add: the unmarked stair with the waltz was never taken

options.moment: followed the arrow past the stair with the music

options.outcome: Down. A small ballroom under dust sheets, and a gramophone playing to nobody. As your eyes settle you see that the sheets are turning, slowly, in pairs. There is nothing here to take and nothing to solve. A second stair leads back up beyond the marked door. The waltz goes round again.
options.moment: walked past the door marked READING ROOM to follow a waltz downstairs

card.title: The Unmarked Stair
card.image: a stair going down into music, with no sign

options.outcome: You stay. One of the dust sheets, passing, makes room for you in the pattern as if it had been keeping your place. The record ends; you wind the gramophone and turn it over, and the other side is the same waltz, slower. When you finally climb the far stair you are not sure how long you were down there, and you do not mind.
options.moment: stayed in the dust-sheet ballroom and turned the record over

options.outcome: Under the sheets: chairs, a dead potted palm, a dance card with every line filled in and no names. Nothing you can use. You go back up the far stair with the particular feeling of having checked.
You take the far stair up and come out beyond the marked door, having seen what was there to be seen. The waltz follows you for a few steps and then lets you go.

The chalk mark was an arrow once, pointing down, and someone has rubbed at it with a sleeve and not quite finished. The waltz is a record: you can hear the needle. Nobody is singing. The smell of rain is real.

seeds.hint: The plate says READING ROOM. The stair says nothing. That is the whole difference between them.
seeds.fallback: The corridor waits. The arrow points. The waltz goes round.
seeds.nudge: The record downstairs reaches its last groove and ticks there, like a patient finger.
seeds.close: The lights in the corridor go out one by one from the stair end, herding you gently to the marked door and through it.
motifs: a door marked with where you were supposed to go
a stair with music and no sign

seeds.title: The Lock With Too Many Answers
seeds.premise: A locked door that can be opened several ways at once. On its brass plate is a numbered dial and a short verse that is a sum in disguise (count the bearers, the doors and the hour on the stopped clock: seven). Above the door an open transom window can be reached by climbing the bookcase. On a stool beside the door sits a keeper in a uniform too large for them, reading a newspaper, with the key on a string round their neck, visibly bored and glad of conversation. Under the stool, for anyone who searches, a spare key hangs on a nail. The hinge pins are on this side. The tension is only which kind of solving the bearer reaches for first and which they stay with when it resists.
seeds.intro: A locked door. On its brass plate there is a dial numbered one to twelve and four lines of verse about bearers, doors and a clock that has stopped. Above the door a small window stands open, and a bookcase leans beside it like an invitation. On a stool, in a uniform two sizes too large, a keeper is reading a newspaper with a key on a string round their neck. They look up, hopefully, and then pretend they did not.
reads: Works the verse and the dial: solve.deduction, solve.linguistic.
Climbs the bookcase to the transom: solve.spatial, solve.execution, risk.
Talks to the keeper, asks for the key, trades news or a joke: solve.social, conflict.negotiation, social toward populated.
Searches and finds the spare key: exploration toward exhaustive.
Takes out the hinge pins, uses the doorknob or the pole, or plays the Joker: solve.lateral; the Joker also evidences willingness to spend.
Which approach they return to after the first fails is stronger evidence than the first try.

options.outcome: The verse is a sum in a costume. One bearer. Five doors you have passed. A clock stopped at one. Seven. You turn the dial to seven and the lock gives with the satisfied click of a thing that has been understood. The keeper lowers the newspaper, a little wistfully.
options.moment: read the verse on the lock as a sum and turned the dial to seven

options.outcome: The bookcase is sturdier than it looks and the window is smaller. There is a moment, halfway through, when you are a cork. Then you are on the far side, upside down, dusty, and through. The keeper applauds twice, drily, from the other side of the door.
options.moment: went over the locked door through the transom

options.outcome: The keeper has been waiting for somebody to ask. They tell you about the crossword, the draught from under the door, and a bearer years ago who climbed through the window and stuck. Then, since you were civil, they take the key off its string and open the door themselves, with a small bow. 'Nobody ever just asks,' they say.

npcs.name: the keeper
npcs.note: opened the door because the bearer asked

options.moment: got through the locked door by asking the keeper

options.outcome: You look properly. The hinge pins are on your side of the door. The clock on the wall has stopped at one. And under the keeper's stool, on a nail, hangs a second key, which the keeper sees you see. 'That one is for emergencies,' they say. 'I suppose you could be one.'

You do not open the lock; you remove the door from the argument. The pins come out, the door leans, and you walk round it. The lock, still firmly locked, hangs in the air attached to nothing, looking like a man who has won a debate in an empty room.
options.moment: ignored the lock and took the door off its hinges

seeds.hint: The keeper turns a page and says, to nobody: 'Four ways through that door that I know of. Five if you count the rude one.'
seeds.fallback: The lock remains locked. The keeper turns a page.
seeds.nudge: The keeper folds the newspaper and looks at you over it, ready to be asked.
seeds.close: The keeper sighs, stands, and unlocks the door. 'Shift change,' they explain, which explains nothing.
motifs: a lock that could be opened four ways
a keeper nobody thought to ask

seeds.title: The Hall That Sends You Back
seeds.premise: A short hall floored with black and white tiles, nine long by three wide, and a door at the far end. Step on a wrong tile and the floor tips the bearer gently back to the start, and the wrong tile stays lit under its glass, a small honest lamp, for next time. Each failure therefore teaches. Two or three attempts are enough to cross. A side passage marked STAFF bypasses the hall through a turnstile that takes one match. The skirting ledge along the wall can also be walked by someone careful. The tension is repeating a hard thing with growing knowledge against paying to skip it against finding another way; and how the bearer takes being sent back.
seeds.intro: A short hall of black and white tiles, nine long, three wide, and a door at the far end. Nothing else, except a side passage marked STAFF with a turnstile and a slot the size of a match. Along the wall, a few of the tiles nearest you are faintly lit from beneath, as if they had been stepped on before, by someone who regretted it.
reads: Steps out, is sent back, and goes again using the lit tile: failure toward failure_as_information (strong on the second and third try), discovery_mastery toward mastery.
Studies the lit tiles before the first step: planning toward deliberative, solve.pattern.
Pays the match at the turnstile, before or after one failure: friction toward low_friction; after a failure also failure toward failure_averse.
Walks the skirting ledge, crawls, throws the doorknob ahead to test tiles: solve.lateral, solve.experimentation.
Curses cheerfully, laughs at being tipped back: tone.funny with failure toward failure_as_information. Annoyance: failure toward failure_averse.

options.outcome: Three tiles in, the floor tilts like a tray and slides you, quite gently, back to the door you came in by. The tile you chose stays lit under its glass. It does not blink. It simply knows.

Again. You know one tile now, and then two, and on the third crossing the pattern stops being a floor and becomes a sentence you can read: white, white, black, and never the one beside a lit one. The far door is under your hand. Behind you the lit tiles go out, one by one, like a marked exam being put away.
options.moment: was sent back to the start twice and crossed on the third try

card.title: The Third Crossing
card.image: a tiled floor with two small lamps lit and a clear path between them

options.outcome: You do not step. You look. The faintly lit tiles near the door are other people's mistakes, and mistakes, read together, are a map. Never the tile beside a lit one. You can see the first four safe steps from here.

One match into the slot. The turnstile takes it with a small dry swallow and lets you through a passage of mops and pipes that comes out beyond the far door. Quick, plain, done. Behind the wall you can hear the tiles, still waiting for someone.

There is a ledge of skirting board a hand wide, and the house, it seems, never thought to tile it. You go along the wall like a burglar, heels over nothing, and step down at the far door having touched no tile at all. The floor seems faintly offended.
options.moment: crossed the tiled hall without touching a single tile

seeds.hint: The lit tiles do not move. Whatever they are telling you, they tell it every time.
seeds.fallback: The tiles wait, black and white, like a question with a great many wrong answers.
seeds.nudge: The turnstile clicks once, by itself, the way a shopkeeper coughs.
seeds.close: Every wrong tile in the hall lights at once, leaving a dark path as plain as a carpet, and you walk it to the far door.
motifs: a door you failed at twice and opened the third time
a floor that kept your mistakes lit

seeds.title: The Hall of Unlabeled Doors
seeds.premise: A corridor with five unlabeled doors, each slightly different, and at the end an open arch that is obviously the way on. Behind the doors, one turn each: a cupboard with a single match on a shelf; a tiny room where it is snowing on an armchair; a wall with a door painted on it; a staircase three steps high up to a window that shows this corridor with the bearer standing in it; a room exactly like the corridor but with six doors. By the arch earlier bearers have chalked how many doors they opened: 0, 2, 5, 5, 1. The tension is how many optional doors the bearer opens, whether they stop after the one reward, and whether they open all five. Curiosity, completionism and fear of missing a reward look the same until the reward has been found.
seeds.intro: A corridor of five doors, none labeled, no two quite alike, and at the far end an open arch with lamplight beyond it: plainly the way on. Beside the arch, at shoulder height, people have chalked numbers, one under another: 0. 2. 5. 5. 1. A stub of chalk sits on the skirting board.
reads: Walks to the arch opening nothing: exploration toward goal_route (strong), pacing toward relentless.
Opens one or two and moves on: mild exploration; note which doors drew them.
Finds the match and stops opening doors: reward.collection or optimization rather than curiosity.
Opens all five: exploration toward exhaustive and reward.completion. If they keep going after being told the rest hold nothing useful, that is curiosity or completionism, not loot-seeking.
Enjoys the painted door or the snowing armchair, sits in the chair: tone.absurd, tone.cozy, pacing toward contemplative.
Chalks their own number, or a false one: reward.expression; a false one is reward.transgression.

options.outcome: You walk the length of the corridor and go under the arch. Five doors watch you pass. You have the sense of a hand hovering over the chalk, ready to write a nought.

threads_add: five unlabeled doors were passed without opening one

options.moment: walked past five unlabeled doors without opening any

options.outcome: Enough doors. You go under the arch, and the corridor behind you settles, the way a room does when a guest has seen as much of it as they are going to.

outcomes: The first door is a cupboard. One shelf. On the shelf, one match, placed dead centre like an exhibit. You take it. The door closes itself behind your hand.
The second door opens on a room the size of a wardrobe where it is snowing, quietly and thoroughly, on an armchair. The snow does not reach the floor. The armchair looks comfortable.
The third door is not a door. It is a very good painting of a door on a wall, with a painted keyhole, and behind the painted keyhole a painted eye, looking faintly sorry about the whole thing.
The fourth door has three steps behind it and at the top a window. Through the window you can see this corridor, from above, and in it a figure at an open door, looking up through a window.
The fifth door opens on this corridor again: same lamps, same arch, same chalk. Except that it has six doors. You count twice. You close it carefully.

options.outcome: You open every one. A cupboard with a match, which you take. A wardrobe room where it snows on an armchair. A painted door with a sorry painted eye. Three steps up to a window showing you, from above, at a window. And the corridor again, with six doors. You close the last one gently. Five. It feels like a finished sum.
options.moment: opened all five unlabeled doors

card.title: The Five Doors
card.image: five doors standing open down a corridor, and a sixth that should not be there

options.outcome: You pick up the chalk and add your number under the others. It looks right there, at the bottom of the column, slightly crooked, yours.

You sit in the armchair. The snow falls on your shoulders and weighs nothing and is not cold. For a little while there is no house, no deck, no errand: only the sound snow makes, which is the sound of nothing being said very well.
options.moment: sat in the armchair in the room where it snows

seeds.hint: The chalked numbers go no higher than five. Somebody, twice, thought five was worth writing down.
seeds.fallback: Five doors. One arch. A stub of chalk. The corridor leaves it to you.
seeds.nudge: The lamplight beyond the arch brightens, the way a host stands up.
seeds.close: The doors close themselves, one after another, down the corridor toward you, and the last one clicks at your heel as you step under the arch.
motifs: doors you opened that led nowhere useful
doors you walked past

seeds.title: The Alcove of Other Nights
seeds.premise: A reading alcove: a lamp, a chair, shelves of ledgers like the one on the counter. Each is one bearer's night in the house, in the Proprietor's hand, and most end with a filled second column. A few stop mid-page. One lies open on the desk: a bearer who wrote back in the margins, arguing with the Proprietor's account of them, and whose last margin note is a question. A clerk made of pigeonholes offers to give the gist of any ledger in one sentence. Nothing here is required. One page, for those who read far enough, mentions that the fourth of anything in this house is the one to watch. The door on is open. The tension is appetite for story against getting on, and which kind of story: people, the place, or what happened next.
seeds.intro: An alcove with a lamp, a chair and shelves of ledgers like the one downstairs. One lies open on the desk. It is somebody's night in this house, set down in the Proprietor's hand, and in the margins a second hand has written back: NOT TRUE. THAT IS NOT WHY. and, lower down, larger, WHO ASKED YOU. A clerk made entirely of pigeonholes rustles in the corner. 'I can give you the gist of any of them,' it offers. 'One sentence. Saves time.' The door beyond stands open.
reads: Sits and reads the open ledger through: narrative toward narrative_first, reward.revelation, pacing toward contemplative.
Asks who the arguing bearer was, what became of them: story.character, story.plot.
Pulls other ledgers, reads about the house itself: story.world, exploration toward exhaustive.
Takes the clerk's one-sentence gist: optimization_expression toward efficiency; narrative only weakly.
Skims for anything useful and leaves: narrative toward systems_first.
Walks through without reading: narrative toward systems_first (moderate), pacing toward relentless.
Writes in a margin themselves: reward.expression, agency toward self_directed, story.emergent.

options.outcome: You sit and read. The Proprietor's account is exact and a little cold: what this bearer opened, what they left, how long they stood at each door. The margins answer back, furious and funny, and by the last page the two hands are almost agreeing. The final margin note is a question: SO WHAT DID I GET. The second column, beside it, has been filled in, and you find you cannot read the word however you tilt the page.
options.moment: sat down and read another bearer's whole night, margins and all

options.outcome: 'That one,' says the clerk, and several of its pigeonholes sigh. 'Opened everything. Argued with everything. Went back twice for a glove. Got what they came for, which was not what they asked for.' It lowers its voice. 'They always think those are different.'

You pull down others. A bearer who never left the first room. A bearer who reached the Reading Room in eleven minutes and was sent back. One ledger is only a list of doors with the same remark beside each: DID NOT. In the oldest, a line underlined twice: IN THIS HOUSE THE FOURTH OF ANYTHING IS THE ONE TO WATCH.

'The gist,' says the clerk, shuffling itself. 'A bearer came, did what they were like, and was told so.' It waits. 'That is the gist of all of them, I am afraid. The details are where the people are.' It seems to feel it has given good value.

There is a pen. Under the other bearer's last question you write an answer of your own. The ink takes a moment to decide whether to dry, and then does. Somewhere overhead, a chair scrapes, as it did downstairs.
options.moment: wrote an answer in the margin of another bearer's ledger

card.title: The Margin
card.image: two kinds of handwriting on one page, and a third, newer

options.outcome: You do not sit. The lamp, the chair and several hundred other people's nights stay exactly where they are, and you go through the open door. The clerk watches you go with the expression of a librarian at closing time.
You close the ledger on its marker and go on through the open door, carrying somebody else's night a little way with you.

seeds.hint: The clerk rustles: 'Reading is not compulsory. Neither is anything else, so far as I have been told.'
seeds.fallback: The lamp burns steadily. The ledgers keep their counsel. The door stays open.
seeds.nudge: The lamp gutters, recovers, and burns a little lower than before.
seeds.close: The lamp goes out with a small apologetic pop, and the only light left is the open door.
motifs: someone else's night, with their objections in the margins
a word in the second column you could not read
